name: Screen printing
summary: Ink pushed through a fine mesh with a squeegee; a stencil on the mesh blocks the parts that do not print.
how: Stretch a silk or polyester mesh of 40–120 threads a centimetre on a frame.
Make the stencil by hand cut film or by a photo emulsion exposed through a film positive.
Pull thick, opaque ink across the screen with a rubber squeegee in one even stroke.
Print each colour from its own screen and let each layer dry before the next.

origin.note: Samuel Simon patents the use of silk as a screen for stencil printing; sign and textile printers take it up.

adoptions.via: Andy Warhol starts to make photographic silkscreens in his studio and prints portraits in flat, loud colour.
Warhol and Rauschenberg pull photo screens onto painted canvas.
Poster studios screen print posters in flat, bright colours for clubs and protests.
The King's Road shop screen prints slogans and images on plain cotton T-shirts for the London punk scene.
Surf and skate labels screen print a name or a mark on the chest of a plain T-shirt and sell it in small runs.
Memphis designers put bold stripes, dots and speckles on ceramic vessels by screen print and decal, and fire the pattern on the glaze.
Dapper Dan prints luxury logos on leather with a silk-screen press and makes jackets and bags of it.
